Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Miguel Soto (Redwood SE), Rina Gupta (Redwood SE), Lena Morris (AtlasPay Head of ML), Samir Patel (AtlasPay Lead Backend), Aisha Khan (AtlasPay CTO), David Cho (AtlasPay SRE)
summary: Intro/demo of Redwood hosted chat API focusing on streaming mechanics, important generation params, retry/backoff and idempotency patterns. Quick tour of Console Optimize suggestions and a plan for a short POC and benchmarks.
topics: Console: per-route telemetry and Optimize suggestions
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jenna Park: Hey everyone! Thanks for joining, we're going to run through a quick hosted chat demo — streaming behavior, how to tune params like temperature and max tokens, and common retry patterns. If anyone needs to jump off at any point, let us know.
[00:00:18] Aisha Khan: Thanks Jenna. We have Lena and Samir on for the ML and backend details, and David for infra questions. We're hoping to get a sense of out-of-the-box latency and failure handling.
[00:00:35] Miguel Soto: Great, I'll share my screen — quick caveat, audio might pop a bit. I'll show a live request to the hosted chat endpoint and then step into how streams arrive client-side.
[00:00:52] Miguel Soto: (shares) So this is a small Node example — we open a streaming connection, we get delta events as they stream in. Important bit: tokens are emitted in chunks, not guaranteed sentence boundaries.
[00:01:09] Samir Patel: How big are the chunks? Is that configurable?
[00:01:15] Miguel Soto: Good question. Chunk size is primarily influenced by the model and network; on Redwood we buffer a small amount server-side to avoid tiny packets but we also expose a streaming window config in the console for host customers. For hosted API the defaults are tuned for low latency; you can opt into slightly larger frames if you prefer throughput.
[00:01:36] Lena Morris: So for us, our UI renders partials as they come — we want low latency but also fewer redraws. Any guidance?
[00:01:45] Rina Gupta: We usually recommend leaving default streaming and then using client-side debounce of 50-150ms for UI updates. If you want fewer chunks, enable the console setting "coalesce-stream-fragments" for the model route and it will batch tokens into ~200ms windows. That reduces redraws and increases throughput slightly.
[00:02:05] David Cho: Does that change billing or just network behavior?
[00:02:09] Miguel Soto: Billing is per token as usual; coalescing doesn't invent tokens, just groups the emissions. So cost unaffected.
[00:02:18] Aisha Khan: Walk us through failure modes — e.g., mid-generation network drop, partial responses — what do we retry?
[00:02:26] Miguel Soto: Two parts: client-side retry vs server-side fallback. If the connection drops mid-stream, you typically retry the request using an idempotency key that includes the last committed user message or last token offset. That lets the server resume or fast-fail and avoid double-charges or duplicate completions. We recommend an idempotency key per user-turn. Also small note — include a max_retries cap and exponential backoff with jitter.
[00:02:52] Samir Patel: How do we resume? Do you expose KV cache resume endpoints?
[00:02:57] Miguel Soto: For hosted, we support resume semantics for a short window using a resume_token returned in the stream metadata. For longer-running or heavy POC, you can use Dedicated where KV cache persistence is configurable.
[00:03:12] Lena Morris: Any gotchas with token counting? If we resume, are we billed twice for overlapping tokens?
[00:03:17] Rina Gupta: We de-duplicate overlap on resume when using the resume_token path. If you simply re-run the same request without idempotency/resume, you may get billed for two completions.
[00:03:28] Miguel Soto: Also, if you request partial streaming and then switch to non-streaming (rare), you should ensure you close the socket cleanly otherwise the server might consider it abandoned.
[00:03:41] Jenna Park: I'll jump in with prompt-level best practices — keep system messages short, steer with examples, and avoid asking for both generation and retrieval in the same call if you want predictable token counts.
[00:03:53] Lena Morris: For temperature and top_p defaults — what should we start with for assistant responses?
[00:03:59] Rina Gupta: For deterministic behavior start with temperature 0.0 to 0.3 and top_p 0.8-0.95. If creative answers are desired, increase temperature to 0.6-0.9. Also consider nucleus sampling with top_p if you need to constrain tail behavior.
[00:04:18] Samir Patel: Max tokens — we expect variable-length outputs; how should we handle truncation?
[00:04:24] Miguel Soto: Two patterns: set a soft max_tokens with a safety cutoff and have the client display a "truncated" indicator or request continuation with conversation state. For safety-critical flows, set a strict max and design follow-up queries.
[00:04:38] David Cho: Are stop sequences supported? We have structured outputs we want to terminate on.
[00:04:42] Rina Gupta: Yes stop sequences are supported. For streaming, the termination token is emitted as part of the final chunk. Sometimes ASR-like transcriptions may mis-label the boundary in the returned event; best practice is to parse the final 'done' event.
[00:04:58] Aisha Khan: Let's talk retries in more detail — patterns you recommend for web services calling Redwood?
[00:05:04] Miguel Soto: Pattern A: For transient 5xx or network errors, use exponential backoff with capped retries (we recommend 3 attempts). Pattern B: For rate-limited 429s, respect Retry-After headers; consider token-bucket client-side to smooth spikes. Pattern C: For deterministic or long-running generation, mark request as idempotent and either resume or ask for a new generation based on the last committed state.
[00:05:30] Samir Patel: Example of idempotency key composition?
[00:05:33] Miguel Soto: Compose as: customer-id + conversation-id + turn-id + request-hash. That keeps it stable across retries and avoids collisions.
[00:05:43] Lena Morris: Any built-in SDK helpers?
[00:05:46] Miguel Soto: Our SDKs include an Idempotency helper and a resume helper for JS and Python. The Console also exposes recommended snippets you can copy.
[00:05:56] Jenna Park: I'm going to show the Console quickly — per-route latency, token breakdowns, and Optimize suggestions. Miguel, can you flip to the Optimize tab?
[00:06:05] Miguel Soto: (switches) Here — Optimize shows suggestions like reducing max_context when you have short prompt histories, enabling quantization for certain model families, and batching window recommendations based on observed QPS. For AtlasPay's conversational throughput, the suggestion is to enable prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[00:06:26] Samir Patel: What's prefix caching?
[00:06:28] Rina Gupta: It's caching the KV cache for identical initial prompt prefixes. If many conversations start with the same system instruction or template, we reuse the cached key-value states which saves compute for the initial tokens. Very helpful for high QPS on similar prompts.
[00:06:43] David Cho: Any limitations around PII and caching? We need to ensure no sensitive data persists.
[00:06:48] Miguel Soto: Cache is configurable by route. By default we do not cache unless you opt-in; for sensitive flows you can set cache: false or configure maskers. We also support request-level directives to avoid caching.
[00:07:01] Aisha Khan: Security questions — SOC 2, data retention, encryption at rest? We have compliance folks who will want the details.
[00:07:07] Jenna Park: We'll send our security pack — SOC 2 Type II, ISO docs, data retention controls, KMS integrations. We can support customer-managed keys in Private deployments and provide audit logs for all request metadata.
[00:07:20] Lena Morris: For the POC, we want to replicate our peak: about 30 QPS with average 150 tokens per exchange. Any immediate red flags?
[00:07:30] Miguel Soto: Hosted can handle that easily with default pool — you'd want to provision Dedicated if you want guaranteed throughput and predictable latency at scale. For a two-week POC, hosted with some autoscaling burst is fine. We'll include cost estimates.
[00:07:44] Samir Patel: Latency numbers for hosted — p90 for a 150-token gen?
[00:07:48] Miguel Soto: Typical p90 is 200-400ms for short responses; for 150 tokens expect token streaming to begin in ~150-350ms and final completion by ~600-900ms depending on model. We'll include model-specific perf numbers in the benchmark doc.
[00:08:06] Aisha Khan: Can we set a hard timeout server-side to ensure we don't hang?
[00:08:10] Rina Gupta: Yes per-route timeout and a client-specified timeout header. We also expose a circuit-breaker config in Console for auto-failover to a cheaper model if latency climbs.
[00:08:21] Jenna Park: Quick demo of a retry case — I'll intentionally drop the connection and show resume token behavior.
[00:08:27] Miguel Soto: (runs) Starting request... emulating network drop... // connection lost // reconnecting... we call resume with resume_token and the server returns remaining tokens; client can append to UI.
[00:08:43] Samir Patel: Nice. How long are resume_tokens valid?
[00:08:46] Miguel Soto: Short-lived by default — about 60 seconds for hosted. You can extend in Dedicated. For UI flows where users might click around, we recommend committing final state server-side and not relying on resume beyond a minute.
[00:08:58] Lena Morris: For the POC we plan mobile clients — flaky networks. Any mobile-specific advice?
[00:09:03] Rina Gupta: Same principles: send idempotency keys, use short-lived resume tokens for immediate reconnects, and implement a client-side queue that retries with backoff. Also consider using a lightweight acknowledgement step when you receive the final 'done' event so you can mark the turn complete server-side.
[00:09:19] David Cho: About billing again — for streaming do we get streamed tokens counts incrementally?
[00:09:24] Miguel Soto: Billing is measured on completion; however you can retrieve token estimates mid-stream via token_event metadata for visibility in dashboards. This is approximate until completion.
[00:09:35] Aisha Khan: We have an internal concern: hallucination on finance data. Any guardrails or safety hooks?
[00:09:41] Rina Gupta: Two approaches: 1) Use retrieval-augmented generation with document embeddings and rerank to ground answers. 2) Use safety prompts and model rollbacks, and enable the Console's quality monitor to alert on regressions from a labelled prompt set. Optimize can suggest quantized models that still perform well on factualness.
[00:10:03] Miguel Soto: We also support a secondary reranker API so you can run candidate outputs and score them against factual checks before returning to users; that adds latency but increases precision.
[00:10:13] Samir Patel: How easy is it to integrate reranker in the stream?
[00:10:17] Miguel Soto: Usually done as a post-generation step. For streaming UIs, you can stream a provisional response and then replace with a reranked final answer or show a confidence badge.
[00:10:27] Lena Morris: Let's talk about SDKs and quickstart — we prefer Python server-side.
[00:10:31] Miguel Soto: Python SDK includes async streaming helpers; we have examples that show reading an async iterator and handling resume tokens. We'll send you a small repo with sample integration.
[00:10:40] Jenna Park: I'll paste links to the quickstart and the benchmark repo in the chat now.
[00:10:44] Miguel Soto: (pastes) Links: quickstart repo, benchmark script, console guide.
[00:10:50] Aisha Khan: Any recommendations for model selection? We care about cost but want high quality on financial semantics.
[00:10:56] Rina Gupta: Start with a mid-sized open model that our catalog flags as finance-tuned; run your labeled prompt set and measure Exact Match / F1 metrics. Optimize will suggest quantization and larger model fallbacks if quality drops below a threshold.
[00:11:11] David Cho: If we go Dedicated later, how disruptive is migration?
[00:11:15] Miguel Soto: Minimal. Same API surface, just point your tenant to the Dedicated endpoint and pin model versions. We handle weights and kernel selection; you'll need to update routing in Console if you manage on-prem.
[00:11:26] Samir Patel: For our POC, can you set up a sandbox tenant with telemetry access for our SREs?
[00:11:32] Jenna Park: Yes, we can create a sandbox org with role-based access and limited quotas. We'll add David and Samir.
[00:11:39] Lena Morris: About logs — request/response logs, are they redacted?
[00:11:43] Miguel Soto: We redact sensitive fields by default and store audit logs separately. You can request full logs under an enterprise agreement with stricter handling.
[00:11:51] Aisha Khan: Are there any known incompatibilities with our stack? We run services in GCP with VPC-SC in some projects.
[00:11:57] Rina Gupta: Hosted works fine with public endpoints; if you need VPC isolation we recommend Private (VPC) deployment or Private control plane. For strict VPC-SC constraints we can discuss a dedicated private lane.
[00:12:07] Samir Patel: Alright — could you outline the POC scope quickly? We want: 2 weeks, 30 QPS synthetic load, labeled prompts, perf and quality metrics.
[00:12:15] Jenna Park: Plan: Week 0 - sandbox tenant + sample prompts + benchmark script; Week 1 - run perf tests and tweak streaming params; Week 2 - quality evals and handoff. We'll produce a short report with latency, cost per 1k tokens, and quality metrics.
[00:12:30] Aisha Khan: Sounds good. Any blockers on your side?
[00:12:34] Jenna Park: None. We'll need the sample prompt set and QPS estimate from Lena.
[00:12:38] Lena Morris: I'll share that by Monday.
[00:12:41] Miguel Soto: One more demo note — we'll show how to change temperature mid-session for follow-up clarifications.
[00:12:46] Miguel Soto: (demo) Start gen at temp 0.2, then issue a follow-up with temp 0.8 for a 'more creative' rewrite — you see how the token distribution changes.
[00:12:59] Samir Patel: And that doesn't change prior tokens or billing, right?
[00:13:03] Rina Gupta: Correct, each generation billed independently.
[00:13:06] David Cho: Are there per-request per-token quotas we should be aware of?
[00:13:10] Miguel Soto: There's a soft max by model; we can increase for Dedicated. For hosted, default max input+output is about 16k tokens for larger families.
[00:13:20] Aisha Khan: Quick question — can we run canary routing to a cheaper model during high load and then fallback?
[00:13:25] Rina Gupta: Yes, Console supports routing policies by latency or cost thresholds; you can set automatic fallback to a cheaper variant when p95 exceeds a threshold.
[00:13:33] Jenna Park: We're at about 13 minutes — do you want us to continue deep dive on any item or move to questions?
[00:13:39] Lena Morris: Let's do a quick Q&A and then wrap.
[00:13:42] Samir Patel: Question — how deterministic are stop sequences under streaming? We've seen partial token emissions that include fragments of a stop token.
[00:13:50] Miguel Soto: The stop token is honored at generation time; sometimes due to chunking you see the token split across two chunks, your client parser should assemble chunk boundaries. The final 'done' event signals deterministic termination.
[00:14:04] Samir Patel: Are there SDK helpers for chunk reassembly?
[00:14:07] Miguel Soto: Yes, the SDK message iterators do reassembly and expose both raw chunks and assembled messages.
[00:14:13] Aisha Khan: How about observability — can we export traces into our existing tracing system?
[00:14:18] Rina Gupta: Yes we have tracing hooks and can export to OTLP. Console also supports per-route traces and spans you can download or forward.
[00:14:26] David Cho: For error rates during heavy bursts, do you provide SLO-based alerts?
[00:14:30] Miguel Soto: Console can create alerts on error rate, latency, and cost spikes. We recommend alerting on 5xx and queue depth when you run high load tests.
[00:14:39] Jenna Park: Wrapping up — we'll send the POC checklist, the security pack, and the benchmark recipe. Anything else from AtlasPay?
[00:14:47] Lena Morris: No, that's good. We'll review and pick a start date.
[00:14:51] Aisha Khan: Thanks everyone.
[00:14:54] Jenna Park: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[00:15:00] [END OF RECORDED TRANSCRIPT - remaining time was used for private sidebars and follow-up scheduling]
